canonicalExplanation.summary: Git keeps **three versions** of your files. **HEAD** is the last commit. The **index** (staging area) is the **exact snapshot you're proposing for the next commit**. The **working tree** is what's on disk right now. `git add` copies **the current content** of a file (or just some of its changes, with `git add -p`) into the index. If you edit the file again afterwards, the index **still holds the older content** until you add again. Compare them with `git diff` (working tree vs index), `git diff --staged` (index vs HEAD) and `git status` (a summary of both).

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner fixes a bug in `score.js` and, in the same file, starts an unfinished experiment. They want to commit only the tested fix. After `git add score.js` they keep editing, and are then surprised that the commit doesn't include their latest changes. Only the tested half of a modified file is staged, so the staged diff differs from the remaining working-tree diff. In this lesson you'll use status and diff variants to explain every changed path before committing.

```predict
{"question": "You `git add notes.md`, then edit notes.md again. What does the next commit contain?", "options": ["The latest version of notes.md", "The version from when you ran git add"], "answer": 1, "why": "git add snapshots content at that moment. Add again to include later edits."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Filesystem and terminal fluency** module and **Repository and working tree** (commits and untracked files).

sections.heading: The model: three snapshots, two diffs
sections.body:
```bash
git add -p score.js        # pick hunks: y for the fix, n for the experiment.
git status
#   Changes to be committed:       modified: score.js   (the fix)
#   Changes not staged for commit: modified: score.js   (the experiment)

git diff --staged          # index vs HEAD: what the commit WILL contain.
git diff                   # working tree vs index: what it will NOT contain.
git restore --staged score.js   # unstage, if you picked wrongly (keeps edits).
```

```text
  HEAD (last commit)  <-- git diff --staged -->  index (proposed)  <-- git diff -->  working tree
```

| Command | Compares |
|---|---|
| `git diff`. | working tree vs index (unstaged). |
| `git diff --staged`. | index vs HEAD (staged). |
| `git diff HEAD`. | working tree vs HEAD (everything). |
| `git status`. | summary of both, plus untracked files. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Can the same file appear in both \"staged\" and \"not staged\" lists?", "answer": "Yes: part of its changes are in the index and more changes exist only in the working tree. That's exactly the tested-fix-plus-experiment situation."}
```

sections.heading: Check before committing

includes: Explain HEAD, the index and the working tree as three separate snapshots.
Stage selectively with git add -p and use status and diff variants to explain every change.

outcomes: Use status and diff variants to explain every changed path before committing.

examples.title: Staging only the tested half
examples.situation: Only the tested half of a modified file is staged, so the staged diff differs from the remaining working-tree diff.
walkthrough: **Stage the tested half:** `git add -p score.js` accepts the fix hunk and skips the experiment hunk.
**Staged diff:** git diff --staged shows only the fix, exactly what the commit will contain.
**Remaining working-tree diff:** git diff shows only the experiment; after committing, git status will still list score.js as modified.
examples.result: The commit contains just the tested fix, and the experiment stays safely uncommitted.

examples.title: The half-committed rename
examples.situation: A learner edits app.js, runs git add app.js, then renames a function in app.js and commits. The build on main breaks because the commit has the old function name in one place and the new one nowhere.
walkthrough: The second edit was never added, so the commit held the earlier snapshot.
git status before committing would have shown app.js in both lists.
Fix: git add the file again (or git add -p), review git diff --staged, then commit.
examples.result: Commits contain complete, consistent snapshots that match what was tested.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Staging marks a filename, so later edits to that file automatically become part of the same staged snapshot.
misconceptions.correction: git add copies the file's content at that moment into the index. Later edits live only in the working tree until you add again, so the next commit uses the older staged content.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, which version did the commit contain?

analogy.example: The index is like **a packed box waiting to be posted**. `git add` puts copies of pages into the box. If you keep editing the page on your desk (working tree), the copy in the box doesn't change. `git commit` seals and posts exactly what's in the box.
limitations: Boxes can't hold half a page; git add -p can stage half a file's changes.
Unpacking the box (restore --staged) doesn't touch your desk.

steps.explanation: Both changes exist only in the working tree.
Only the tested half of a modified file is staged.
The staged diff differs from the remaining working-tree diff.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing selective staging. Step 1, Edit: working tree is fix + experiment; index is same as HEAD. Both changes exist only in the working tree. Step 2, Stage: index is HEAD + fix. Only the tested half of a modified file is staged. Step 3, Compare: diff --staged is fix; diff is experiment. The staged diff differs from the remaining working-tree diff.

faded.prompt: For "Staging only the tested half", explain why when only the tested half of a modified file is staged, the staged diff differs from the remaining working-tree diff.
expectedEvidence: Names the example "Staging only the tested half": score.js held a fix and an experiment.
Only the tested half of a modified file is staged.
The staged diff differs from the remaining working-tree diff.
The commit contains just the tested fix.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable repo, change two lines in one file, stage only one with git add -p, and write what git status, git diff and git diff --staged each show.
scaffold: Answer y for one hunk, n for the other.
Split hunks with s if needed.
expectedEvidence: File appears in both status lists.
Each diff shows exactly one change.

farTransfer.prompt: Make three kinds of change in a disposable repo: a staged edit, an unstaged edit to the same file, and an untracked new file. Explain every path shown by git status, then produce a commit containing only the staged edit and verify with git show.
scaffold: Use git diff HEAD for the full picture.
expectedEvidence: The commit contains only the intended change.

remediation.explanation: Before every commit run **git status, then git diff --staged**. Ask: **is this exactly what I tested and meant to record?** If not, add, add -p or restore --staged until it is.

recap.summary: To explain every changed path before committing, remember HEAD is the last commit, the index is the proposed next snapshot filled by git add at that moment, and the working tree is what's on disk; use git diff for unstaged changes, git diff --staged for what will be committed, and git status for the summary.
